claims.text: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has poor oxygen resistance.
A thin, high-purity Hf coating on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective HfO2 scale during high-temperature exposure.
The Hf coating can overcome poor oxygen resistance without degrading the alloy's intrinsic mechanical performance.
Hot-press sintering can produce an approximately 120 μm Hf coating with coating–substrate interdiffusion.
High-temperature processing will produce an interdiffused Hf-based transition layer in coated HfNbTaTiZr.
Zr diffusion into the Hf coating can form an HfZr-like transition layer.
The HfZr transition layer chemically bonds the Hf coating to the high-entropy-alloy substrate.
The interdiffused transition layer facilitates formation of a dense, adherent HfO2 scale.
The Hf coating oxidizes at high temperature to form a continuous, dense HfO2 layer.
The HfO2 layer acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and protects the substrate from further oxidation.
The interdiffused transition layer provides mechanical continuity.
Mechanical continuity at the interface will minimize losses in ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
After exposure in air at about 1000 °C for up to 5 hours, the coated alloy will have significantly lower oxidation weight gain than the uncoated alloy.
After exposure, the coated alloy will show fewer visible signs of oxidation than the uncoated alloy.
The coated alloy will retain room-temperature ductility and yield strength at 1000 °C relative to uncoated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Uncoated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr undergoes rapid oxidation and mechanical-property degradation during high-temperature exposure to oxygen.
Nonuniform coating, inadequate interdiffusion, excessive thickness, or thermally induced delamination could compromise protection.
Failure to reduce oxidation weight gain by at least 40% relative to an uncoated control, or significant degradation of mechanical properties, would falsify the hypothesis.
